Content:
The hyperbolic functions are functions defined using the exponential functions [MATH: e^x] and [MATH: e^{-x}.] As we will see at the end of the lesson, hyperbolic functions are closely related to trigonometric functions.

Content:
The hyperbolic cosine (abbreviated and pronounced "cosh") is defined as
[MATH: \cosh x= \dfrac12\left(e^x+e^{-x}\right).]

Content:
The graph of [MATH: y=\cosh x] is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/633536fd191be96b6c71bcd5a44dddfb]

Content:
The function [MATH: y=\cosh x] is not a parabola, although it may look like one.

Content:
Note the following properties of [MATH: y=\cosh x\mathbin{:}]

Content:
- Its domain is [MATH: x\in (-\infty, \infty).]
- Its range is [MATH: y \geq 1.]
- It is an even function.

Content:
To evaluate [MATH: \cosh x] at some value, say [MATH: x=2,] we simply substitute our value into the definition:

Content:
[MATH: \cosh 2 = (1)/(2)(e^{2} + e^{− 2}) ≈ 3.7622]

items.title: Evaluating Hyperbolic Cosine

sections.normalized_html: Evaluate [MATH: \cosh (\ln 2).]
EXPLANATION

The definition of [MATH: \cosh{x}] is [MATH: \cosh{x} = \dfrac{1}{2}(e^{x} + e^{-x}).]

Therefore, [MATH: \cosh (\ln 2)|= (1)/(2)(e^{\ln 2} + e^{− \ln 2}); = (1)/(2)(e^{\ln 2} + e^{\ln 2^{− 1}}); = (1)/(2)(2 + 2^{− 1}); = (1)/(2)(2 + (1)/(2)); = (1)/(2)((4 + 1)/(2)); = (5)/(4).]

Therefore,

items.title: Evaluating Hyperbolic Sine

sections.normalized_html: Evaluate [MATH: \sinh 1.]
EXPLANATION

The definition of [MATH: \sinh x] is [MATH: \sinh{x} = \dfrac{1}{2}(e^{x} - e^{-x}).]

Therefore, [MATH: \sinh 1|= (1)/(2)(e^{1} − e^{− 1}); = (1)/(2)(e − (1)/(e)); = (1)/(2)((e^{2} − 1)/(e)); = (e^{2} − 1)/(2e).]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Just as we do with trigonometric functions, we can use the basic hyperbolic functions [MATH: \sinh x] and [MATH: \cosh x] to create more hyperbolic functions.

Content:
The hyperbolic tangent (pronounced "tanch") is defined as
[MATH: \tanh x = (\sinh x)/(\cosh x)|= (e^{x} − e^{− x})/(e^{x} + e^{− x}).]
The graph of [MATH: y=\tanh x] is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f4ad6bdfbacc1b12b49187a13ff057aa]

Content:
Note the following properties of [MATH: y=\tanh x\mathbin{:}]

Content:
- Its domain is [MATH: x\in (-\infty, \infty).]
- Its range is [MATH: y \in (-1,1).]
- It has horizontal asymptotes [MATH: y=\pm 1.]
- It is an odd function.

Content:
We can write down an equivalent definition of [MATH: \tanh{x}] by multiplying the numerator and denominator by [MATH: e^x\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: \tanh x|= (e^{x} − e^{− x})/(e^{x} + e^{− x}); = (e^{x} − e^{− x})/(e^{x} + e^{− x}) ⋅ (e^{x})/(e^{x}); = (e^{2x} − 1)/(e^{2x} + 1)]
The third definition of [MATH: \tanh{x}] can be found by multiplying the numerator and denominator of our original definition by [MATH: e^{-x}\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: \tanh x|= (e^{x} − e^{− x})/(e^{x} + e^{− x}); = (e^{x} − e^{− x})/(e^{x} + e^{− x}) ⋅ (e^{− x})/(e^{− x}); = (1 − e^{− 2x})/(1 + e^{− 2x})]

Content:
We can use any definition of [MATH: \tanh x] that we like for a given situation. However, it's often convenient to use the second or third definition when evaluating a function containing [MATH: \tanh{x},] because they include fewer exponential terms than the first definition.

items.title: Evaluating Hyperbolic Tangent

sections.normalized_html: Evaluate [MATH: \tanh{4}.]
EXPLANATION

The definition of [MATH: \tanh x] is

[MATH: \tanh x|= (e^{x} − e^{− x})/(e^{x} + e^{− x}); = (e^{2x} − 1)/(e^{2x} + 1); = (1 − e^{− 2x})/(1 + e^{− 2x}).] Using the second definition, we get

[MATH: \tanh 4|= (e^{2(4)} − 1)/(e^{2(4)} + 1); = (e^{8} − 1)/(e^{8} + 1).]

There is a deep connection between trigonometric and hyperbolic functions. This means that we can use a lot of our knowledge of trigonometry to solve problems containing hyperbolic functions.

Content:
To see how they are connected, we need to go back to Euler's formula:

Content:
[MATH: e^{\textrm i\theta} = \cos\theta + \textrm i\sin\theta]

Content:
By replacing [MATH: \theta] with [MATH: -\theta,] we get

Content:
[MATH: e^{-\textrm i\theta} = \cos\theta - \textrm i\sin\theta.]

Content:
Adding the two equations gives

Content:
[MATH: e^{\textrm i\theta} + e^{-\textrm i\theta} = 2\cos\theta.]

Content:
Making [MATH: \cos\theta] the subject, we get

Content:
[MATH: \cos\theta = \dfrac12\left(e^{\textrm i\theta} + e^{-\textrm i\theta}\right).]

Content:
Notice that the right-hand side is identical to [MATH: \cosh(\textrm i\theta).] This means that we have the identity

Content:
[MATH: \cos\theta = \cosh(\textrm i\theta).]

We can write down an equivalent definition of [MATH: \tanh{x}] by multiplying the numerator and denominator by [MATH: e^x\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: \tanh x|= (e^{x} − e^{− x})/(e^{x} + e^{− x}); = (e^{x} − e^{− x})/(e^{x} + e^{− x}) ⋅ (e^{x})/(e^{x}); = (e^{2x} − 1)/(e^{2x} + 1)]
The third definition of [MATH: \tanh{x}] can be found by multiplying the numerator and denominator of our original definition by [MATH: e^{-x}\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: \tanh x|= (e^{x} − e^{− x})/(e^{x} + e^{− x}); = (e^{x} − e^{− x})/(e^{x} + e^{− x}) ⋅ (e^{− x})/(e^{− x}); = (1 − e^{− 2x})/(1 + e^{− 2x})]

Content:
We can use any definition of [MATH: \tanh x] that we like for a given situation. However, it's often convenient to use the second or third definition when evaluating a function containing [MATH: \tanh{x},] because they include fewer exponential terms than the first definition.

Item 13 — Tutorial: The Relationship Between Trigonometric and Hyperbolic Cosine

Content:
There is a deep connection between trigonometric and hyperbolic functions. This means that we can use a lot of our knowledge of trigonometry to solve problems containing hyperbolic functions.

Content:
To see how they are connected, we need to go back to Euler's formula:

Content:
[MATH: e^{\textrm i\theta} = \cos\theta + \textrm i\sin\theta]

Content:
By replacing [MATH: \theta] with [MATH: -\theta,] we get

Content:
[MATH: e^{-\textrm i\theta} = \cos\theta - \textrm i\sin\theta.]

Content:
Adding the two equations gives

Content:
[MATH: e^{\textrm i\theta} + e^{-\textrm i\theta} = 2\cos\theta.]

Content:
Making [MATH: \cos\theta] the subject, we get

Content:
[MATH: \cos\theta = \dfrac12\left(e^{\textrm i\theta} + e^{-\textrm i\theta}\right).]

Content:
Notice that the right-hand side is identical to [MATH: \cosh(\textrm i\theta).] This means that we have the identity

Content:
[MATH: \cos\theta = \cosh(\textrm i\theta).]

Item 14 — Tutorial: The Relationship Between Trigonometric and Hyperbolic Sine

Content:
We can similarly derive a link between [MATH: \sin\theta] and [MATH: \sinh\theta.] To do this, let's recall Euler's formula once more.

Content:
[MATH: e^{\textrm i\theta} = \cos\theta + \textrm i\sin\theta]

Content:
We also have

Content:
[MATH: e^{-\textrm i\theta} = \cos\theta - \textrm i\sin\theta.]

Content:
Subtracting the two equations, we get

Content:
[MATH: e^{\textrm i\theta} - e^{-\textrm i\theta} = 2\textrm i\sin\theta.]

Content:
Making [MATH: \sin\theta] the subject of the equation, we get

Content:
[MATH: \sin θ|= (1)/(2\textrm{i})(e^{\textrm{i}θ} − e^{− \textrm{i}θ}); = − (\textrm{i})/(2)(e^{\textrm{i}θ} − e^{− \textrm{i}θ}),]

Content:
which gives us the identity

Content:
[MATH: \sin\theta = -\textrm i \sinh(\textrm i\theta).]
